summary: Describes conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo structure from RFC 5958, and for protecting the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type with various Cryptographic Message Syntax types. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Instructions on which locks to use for the box that holds a secret key.

questions: how to encrypt a private key with a password
which algorithms protect asymmetric key packages
what is aes key wrap with padding
subtitle: Which cryptographic algorithms to use when protecting private keys and key packages with CMS.

tldr.problem: Private keys and key packages need protecting in transit and at rest, but RFC 5958 leaves open which algorithms an implementation should support for that.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5959 picks existing algorithms: password-based encryption with PBES2 for EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo, and per-type MUST and SHOULD lists for the CMS types that can wrap an AsymmetricKeyPackage. It defines no new algorithms.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that implementations of CMS-protected key packages are recommended to follow. It has been updated by RFC 6162.

today: RFC 5959 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6162. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 5959 describes conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo structure from RFC 5958. That structure is used by PKCS #12 to encrypt a PrivateKeyInfo. Like EncryptedData in RFC 5652, it has no recipients, no originators and no content encryption keys, so keys must be managed by other means.

It also covers the conventions needed to protect the AsymmetricKeyPackage content type with Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) types: SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthenticatedData and AuthEnvelopedData. Implementations of AsymmetricKeyPackage do not have to support any CMS protecting type, but if a package is CMS protected, following these conventions is RECOMMENDED.

The document defines no new algorithms. It refers to previously defined ones.
sections.eli5: When you put a secret key in a locked box, you need to agree on which locks to use. This paper only picks from locks that already exist.

sections.title: Encrypting a Private Key with a Password
sections.content:
The de facto standard for encrypting the PrivateKeyInfo that goes into the encryptedData field is Password Based Encryption (PBE) from PKCS #5 (RFC 2898) and PKCS #12. The main difference between the two is how the password is encoded: ASCII for PKCS #5 and Unicode for PKCS #12.

RFC 2898 defines two schemes, PBES1 and PBES2, and recommends PBES2 for new specifications. Implementations MUST support PBES2 with the PBKDF2 key derivation function using HMAC with SHA-256 and with AES Key Wrap with Padding as the encryption algorithm. They MAY also support AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding.
sections.eli5: A password is turned into a strong key, and that key locks up the secret. Everyone must at least know the standard recipe for doing this.

sections.title: Algorithms for Each CMS Protecting Type
sections.content:
For each CMS type an implementation chooses to support, RFC 5959 sets MUST and SHOULD algorithms.

  • SignedData: RSA MUST be supported; RSASSA-PSS and DSA SHOULD be. SHA-256 MUST be supported, and SHA-1 SHOULD be.
  • EnvelopedData: key transport MUST be implemented and key agreement MAY be. For key transport, RSA encryption MUST be supported and RSAES-OAEP SHOULD be. For key agreement, ephemeral-static Diffie-Hellman MUST be supported. In every case AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding MUST be supported as the content encryption algorithm, and AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding SHOULD be. With key agreement, the key wrap algorithm must match the content encryption algorithm.
  • EncryptedData: AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding MUST be implemented and AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding SHOULD be.
  • AuthenticatedData: SHA-256 MUST be implemented and SHA-1 SHOULD be, as the digest. HMAC with SHA-256 MUST be supported and HMAC with SHA-1 SHOULD be.
  • AuthEnvelopedData: follow the EnvelopedData recommendations, except that the content encryption algorithm MUST be AES-GCM, with the 128-bit version required and the 256-bit version recommended. AES-CCM MAY also be supported.

The key-wrap choice is deliberate: since the content is itself a cryptographic key, the RFC uses an algorithm traditionally used to encrypt one key with another.
sections.eli5: There are five kinds of box. For each one, the paper says which locks every maker must know, which they should know and which are optional extras.

sections.title: Public Key Sizes
sections.content: The easiest way to implement SignedData, EnvelopedData and AuthEnvelopedData is with public key certificates (RFC 5280). An implementation that supports RSA, RSASSA-PSS, DSS, RSAES-OAEP or DH MUST support key lengths from 1024 bits to 2048 bits, inclusive.
sections.eli5: Locks come in different sizes. Every maker must at least be able to handle the small and medium ones named in the paper.

sections.title: SMIMECapabilities Values
sections.content: RFC 5751 defines the SMIMECapabilities attribute, which lets a recipient advertise the algorithms it supports. RFC 5959 supplies the encoded values for AES Key Wrap with Padding when used as a content encryption algorithm, one each for the AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 variants. They differ only in their last byte: 08, 1C and 30 respectively.
sections.eli5: It is like a name tag that says which locks you can handle, so that people sending you a box can pick one you understand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the referenced algorithm and CMS documents apply. The RFC adds that password-based encryption is only as strong as its weakest link, the password, which must have enough entropy to resist guessing. Citing NIST SP 800-63, it says a user-chosen 20-character password from a 94-character keyboard with no checks gives 36 bits of entropy, and a randomly chosen one gives roughly 131 bits.

The key-wrap algorithms were chosen following RFC 5649, which values using a mechanism solely for protecting keying material. The RFC notes that no AES-GCM or AES-CCM mode provides the same property, and says the document will be updated if one is defined. NIST SP 800-57 is cited for comparing key sizes and security levels.
sections.eli5: A strong lock does not help if the password is easy to guess. Long, random passwords are much harder to guess than ones people make up.
